embedded.caption: Stowers et al. (2017), Supplementary Video 7. Zebrafish responses to real and virtual posts.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative interface experiment: Stowers and colleagues present real and virtual posts to zebrafish. The recording concerns computer-controlled visual structure, not a sea lion touchscreen. EVE converts button contact into cursor movement; this preparation relates the animal’s position to rendered visual structure. A rendered stimulus is therefore distinct from an input device. The comparison does not claim reward learning in this fish recording.

embedded.credit: Rouse AA, Cook PF, Large EW, Reichmuth C (2016). Beat Keeping in a Sea Lion As Coupled Oscillation: Implications for Comparative Understanding of Human Rhythm. Frontiers in Neuroscience 10:257. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2016.00257
embedded.caption: Rouse et al. (2016), article-provided video: Video1.MP4. Sea-lion rhythmic responding.
embedded.teaching_note: Sea-lion comparison: Ronan’s trained rhythmic head movements were studied while the sound sequence changed in phase or tempo. The paper tested adjustment of response timing after a perturbation, rather than cursor navigation. EVE’s success tone marks a completed action; the rhythm study’s repeated sounds supply timing information during an ongoing action. A sound associated with a task can therefore have different roles depending on the preparation. The movement data support behavioral timing adjustment, while coupled oscillation is a model of those data rather than a direct neuronal recording.
embedded.reference: Rouse AA, Cook PF, Large EW, Reichmuth C (2016). Beat Keeping in a Sea Lion As Coupled Oscillation: Implications for Comparative Understanding of Human Rhythm. Frontiers in Neuroscience 10:257. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2016.00257

embedded.caption: Portugues & Engert (2011), Movie S1. Tail movements and closed-loop gratings.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative feedback preparation: Portugues and Engert record zebrafish tail movements and visually controlled gratings. Closed-loop presentation relates the animal’s own movement to the stimulus it receives. In EVE, visual cursor feedback instead follows directional-button input. These distinct preparations separate response production from the sensory consequence used to adjust the next action. The tail movement is not a touchscreen response.
embedded.credit: Portugues R, Engert F (2011). Adaptive locomotor behavior in larval zebrafish. Frontiers in systems neuroscience 5:72. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnsys.2011.00072

embedded.caption: Stowers et al. (2017), Supplementary Video 13. Zebrafish portals and virtual swarms.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative animal-controlled visual environment: zebrafish move among rendered agents and portals in Stowers and colleagues’ study. Entering a portal changes the presented virtual world. EVE changes target position while retaining the cursor-to-button relationship. Both preparations couple animal behavior to software-defined visual conditions, but their motor actions and reward arrangements differ. The fish footage is not evidence of sea-lion learning.

embedded.caption: Zebunke et al. (2018), Supplementary Video 3. Switching from waiting to the immediate reward.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative change of choice: a pig interrupts waiting and switches to the immediately available reward in Zebunke and colleagues’ study. The change ends the opportunity for the larger delayed reward. In the EVE failure condition, an incorrect choice ends that trial’s opportunity for reward. These are different contingencies: the pig can select another reward, whereas the failed EVE trial supplies none. The shared teaching issue is how the current response changes the remaining opportunity.

embedded.caption: Zebunke et al. (2018), Supplementary Video 1. Waiting for the delayed reward.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative reward-choice experiment: Zebunke and colleagues record a pig waiting for a delayed reward. Lack of active input can be a behavior within the task rather than disengagement. In this study, waiting retained access to a larger delayed reward. In EVE, noncontact latency is measured separately from button contact; the two studies give different meanings to a pause because their contingencies differ.

embedded.caption: Joly et al. (2014), Movie S1. Mouse-lemur touchscreen discrimination.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative touchscreen preparation: the published Movie S1 contains four trials of visual discrimination by a young grey mouse lemur. The touchscreen and two response windows are at the upper end of the field of view, while the reward tray lies outside the field of view at the opposite end. The paper also tested reversal of the rewarded visual discrimination. The movie records ordinary discrimination trials, not an explicitly identified reversal session. This direct screen response differs from the harbor seal’s physical response targets and the EVE directional controller.

embedded.teaching_note: Comparative reward-delivery experiment: a pig chooses the immediately available option rather than waiting for the larger reward in Zebunke and colleagues’ study. The response determines which reward can be obtained. This differs from EVE’s automatic delivery after successful target contact. The recording concerns a delay-choice preparation and must not be interpreted as a sea-lion preference measurement.
